In this article we present the basic methods of Cartan's moving frame method, and we apply it to classical theory of surfaces. Of importance is the use of exterior differential applied to systems of equations.

1. Frames and co-frames in a tangent space

An frame at a point p∈R3 {p\in\mathbb{R}^{3}}p∈R3 is a choice of a basis in the tangent space TpR3≅R3 {T_{p}\mathbb{R}^{3}\cong\mathbb{R}^{3}}Tp​R3≅R3. The frame is called orthonormal if the basis is orthonormal. We would like to think of a frame E {E}E as a row of basis vectors, that is

E=(E1E2E3),Ei∈TpR3(1) \displaystyle E=\begin{pmatrix}E_{1} & E_{2} & E_{3}\end{pmatrix},\quad E_{i}\in T_{p}\mathbb{R}^{3} (1)E=(E1​​E2​​E3​​),Ei​∈Tp​R3(1)

and if Ei {E^{i}}Ei's are consistently represented as column vectors in R3 {\mathbb{R}^{3}}R3, we can then identify E {E}E with an element in the general linear group GL(3,R) {GL(3,\mathbb{R})}GL(3,R), or in the case of an orthonormal frame, the orthogonal group O(3,R) {O(3,\mathbb{R})}O(3,R). We shall almost always deal with orthonormal frames, so frames mentioned below the fold are always othonormal, if not specified.

For another frame F {F}F, we have the transformation rule

F=EAT,A∈O(3).(2) \displaystyle F=EA^{T},\quad A\in O(3). (2)F=EAT,A∈O(3).(2)

That A {A}A ``acts on the right hand side'' is to represent the fact that basis vectors of F {F}F is obtained from linear combination of basis vectors of E {E}E, and clearly this is due to the convention that we represent E {E}E in the way of (1).

At the same time we can consider the co-frame θ {\theta}θ of a frame E {E}E. This is a set of 1-forms, or dual basis vectors of those of E {E}E, namely they should satisfy the real-linear duality

θi(Ej)=⟨Ej,θi⟩=δji={1if i=j0othewise,(3) \displaystyle \theta^{i}(E_{j})=\langle E_{j},\theta^{i}\rangle=\delta_{j}^{i}=\begin{cases} 1 & \text{if }i=j\\ 0 & \text{othewise} \end{cases}, (3)θi(Ej​)=⟨Ej​,θi⟩=δji​={10​if i=jothewise​,(3)

and for all a,b∈R {a,b\in\mathbb{R}}a,b∈R

⟨Ek,aθi+bθj⟩=a⟨Ek,θi⟩+b⟨Ek,θj⟩,⟨aEi+bEj,θk⟩=a⟨Ei,θk⟩+b⟨Ej,θk⟩.\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} \langle E_{k},a\theta^{i}+b\theta^{j}\rangle & = & a\langle E^{k},\theta_{i}\rangle+b\langle E^{k},\theta_{j}\rangle,\\ \langle aE_{i}+bE_{j},\theta^{k}\rangle & = & a\langle E_{i},\theta^{k}\rangle+b\langle E_{j},\theta^{k}\rangle. \end{array}⟨Ek​,aθi+bθj⟩⟨aEi​+bEj​,θk⟩​==​a⟨Ek,θi​⟩+b⟨Ek,θj​⟩,a⟨Ei​,θk⟩+b⟨Ej​,θk⟩.​

Both θi(Ej) {\theta^{i}(E_{j})}θi(Ej​) and ⟨Ej,θi⟩ {\langle E_{j},\theta^{i}\rangle}⟨Ej​,θi⟩ will be used to denote the linear duality pairing, whenever which is more notationally convenient.

We would like to think of θ {\theta}θ as a column of forms, that is

θ=(θ1θ2θ3),\displaystyle \theta=\begin{pmatrix}\theta^{1}\\ \theta^{2}\\ \theta^{3} \end{pmatrix},θ=​θ1θ2θ3​​,

and if θi {\theta^{i}}θi's are consistently represented as row vectors in R3 {\mathbb{R}^{3}}R3, we can again identify θ {\theta}θ with an element in the orthogonal group O(3,R) {O(3,\mathbb{R})}O(3,R). Now of course, the transformation rule has to be deduced from (1) and (3): Let ξ {\xi}ξ be the co-frame of F {F}F. If E {E}E is transformed to F {F}F according to (2), the corresponding transformation rule for θ {\theta}θ is then

ξ=(AT)−1θ=Aθ.\displaystyle \xi=(A^{T})^{-1}\theta=A\theta.ξ=(AT)−1θ=Aθ.

To see this, we can check by writing the (i,j) {(i,j)}(i,j)-th entry of A {A}A to be Aji {A_{j}^{i}}Aji​, and compute, for example

ξ1(F1)=⟨(AT)1iEi,Ai1θi⟩=∑i=13Ai1Ai1=1,\displaystyle \xi^{1}(F_{1})=\langle(A^{T})_{1}^{i}E_{i},A{}_{i}^{1}\theta^{i}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{3}A_{i}^{1}A_{i}^{1}=1,ξ1(F1​)=⟨(AT)1i​Ei​,Ai1​θi⟩=i=1∑3​Ai1​Ai1​=1,

here repeated indices appearing both in upper and lower slots but without summation sign is a short hand for summation on that index, namely

Ai1θi:=A11θ1+A21θ2+A31θ3.\displaystyle A_{i}^{1}\theta^{i}:=A_{1}^{1}\theta^{1}+A_{2}^{1}\theta^{2}+A_{3}^{1}\theta^{3}.Ai1​θi:=A11​θ1+A21​θ2+A31​θ3.

We shall be using this convention throughout this article.

Why should we be using forms? One of the reasons is that they are objects that can be pulled back by corresponding morphisms from the space they lie in. More precisely, suppose T:V→W {T:V\rightarrow W}T:V→W is a linear map between vector spaces, and θ1 {\theta^{1}}θ1 is a 1-form on W {W}W. Then there is a form T∗θ1 {T^{*}\theta^{1}}T∗θ1 defined naturally on V {V}V, via

⟨Ei,T∗(θ1)⟩=⟨T(Ei),θ1⟩.\displaystyle \langle E_{i},T^{*}(\theta^{1})\rangle=\langle T(E^{i}),\theta_{1}\rangle.⟨Ei​,T∗(θ1)⟩=⟨T(Ei),θ1​⟩.

Vectors and forms can all be ecapsulated in the unified concept of tensors. This concept is already implicit in the above, in the form of a row of vectors E {E}E, or of a column of 1-forms θ {\theta}θ, or of a linear map A {A}A. In fact, they are all tensors of type (1,1) {(1,1)}(1,1). More generally, multilinear maps are also tensors. But we won't need to use tensors in its full power so it suffices to settle down with the above concepts for now.

2. Differentiating a frame field in R3 {\mathbb{R}^{3}}R3

Let t↦γ(t) {t\mapsto\gamma(t)}t↦γ(t) a smooth curve in R3 {\mathbb{R}^{3}}R3, with γ(0)=p {\gamma(0)=p}γ(0)=p, γ′(0)=v {\gamma'(0)=v}γ′(0)=v, called a directional vector at p {p}p. Since we are in the Euclidean space, by using the Cartesian coordinate of an open neighborhood U {U}U of p {p}p, we can also consider a frame field in U {U}U, and again with the identification of all tangent spaces TxR3 {T_{x}\mathbb{R}^{3}}Tx​R3 by translations, we have the equation

E(x)=E(p)A(x)T,x∈U.(4) \displaystyle E(x)=E(p)A(x)^T,\quad x\in U. (4)E(x)=E(p)A(x)T,x∈U.(4)

Now let us make two important observations:

  • For a fixed v,x {v,x}v,x, the mapping E(x)↦∇vE(x) {E(x)\mapsto\nabla_{v}E(x)}E(x)↦∇v​E(x) is linear;

Equivalently, the value of ωji {\omega_{j}^{i}}ωji​ is given by the Euclidean inner product of ∇vEi {\nabla_{v}E_{i}}∇v​Ei​ and Ej {E_{j}}Ej​

Definition 1 (Connection form) The matrix-valued 1-form ω {\omega}ω defined as above is called the connection form in the Euclidean space. The quantities

Γkijk:=⟨Ei,(ωT)jk⟩=∇EiEj⋅Ek\displaystyle \Gamma_{\phantom{k}ij}^{k}:=\langle E_{i},(\omega^{T})_{j}^{k}\rangle=\nabla_{E_{i}}E_{j}\cdot E_{k}Γkijk​:=⟨Ei​,(ωT)jk​⟩=∇Ei​​Ej​⋅Ek​
